lead: Before you sign, every screen has to show you something true. Check each instrument against something you can see, set it up for your week, and learn the radio while the technician is aboard.

sections.title: A chart for every mile, a fix you have checked
refs: Check-in: chart coverage vs cruising area
Check-in: GPS fix at the berth

blocks.p: Ask of the chart card: does it cover **the whole cruising ground** the contract allows, and how old is it? A base map without depths is not a chart. Paper chart and pilot book are the backup and hold the harbour detail: ask for current ones.

fig.note: Plotter screen at the berth, Sat 17:00

blocks.cap: Without satellites the plotter shows its last stored position.

blocks.p: Wait for the fix and see the boat on its berth. GPS positions are on the **WGS84** datum; an older paper chart on another datum prints the shift to apply.

sections.title: Make the plotter yours before you leave

head: Setting
What you want
rows: Nautical miles, knots and metres, as on the chart
The last crew's cleared, your own built from the chart
Where you have been: your way back out in the dark
Drops a mark, shows bearing and distance back to it

blocks.p: Have the technician show how **MOB** marks and clears, then brief the crew. It is for one thing only: an anchorage is an ordinary waypoint, and on some sets MOB also sends an alert.

sections.title: Know what each number is measured from
refs: SOG vs speed through the water
Check-in: radar and defects on the form

blocks.p: Compare the sounder with the harbour plan. A reading three times too big is in feet. With no offset it reads **below the transducer**, not the keel: with a draught of 2.1 m and the transducer 0.4 m down, the keel touches at a reading of 1.7 m. Set the shallow alarm a metre or more above that.

lines: Through the water 6.0, over the ground 4.2
The difference: 1.8 kn of current against you

blocks.p: The **log** is a paddle wheel, speed through the water; **SOG** is GPS speed over the ground. The difference is current, and a log at zero under way is a fouled wheel. Plan arrivals by SOG: 24 miles at 4 knots is six hours.

A wild wind reading in a calm is often a halyard round the masthead unit. A number missing at one display but shown at another is the network, not the sensor. On a catamaran ask which readouts repeat at the second helm.

blocks.rule: A dead instrument goes on the form as unserviceable, so it is not charged to you. Weigh it against your plan: no depth, no anchoring; radar matters at night and in fog.

sections.title: What still works when the screen goes dark

blocks.cap: 090° by compass plus 3°E variation is 093° true; the other 5° is deviation.

blocks.p: On the test run, with no current running, compare the **steering compass** with the plotter's course over the ground. What variation does not explain is deviation, often a phone by the binnacle. A hand-bearing compass has no deviation card: use it at the bow, away from iron.

A tablet is a backup only with offline charts and a 12 V lead. A phone app is a third source: it overheats, goes flat, and its depths may be unsurveyed. Keep the **log book** daily: times, positions, engine hours, weather, breakages. From the briefing take the local wind and the currents in channels.

sections.title: Helpers that still need a lookout
refs: AIS — CPA alarm and guard zone

blocks.p: See **Standby**, a course change and the alarm on the test run. The autopilot steers a heading, not round boats: in harbours and anchorages a person steers. In wind mode it holds the apparent wind angle, so it follows every shift: watch the course. If its heading disagrees with compass and plotter, the base calibrates it.

fig.note: CPA alarm: it sounds while there is time to act

blocks.p: Ask whether the **AIS** only receives or is a transponder: a receiver shows the ferries to you, only a transponder shows you to them. For a night passage set a CPA alarm wide enough to act on and audible at the helm.

sections.title: Set the radio up and learn its keys
refs: VHF licence — operator and ship station
DSC — cancelling a false distress alert

blocks.p: Under way you keep a watch on **channel 16**, with dual watch on the base's channel and the squelch just above the hiss; in harbour the set may go off. Make the radio check on a working channel, never on 16, with a station miles away: across the pontoon it says nothing about the antenna. Use 1 W in harbour, 25 W at sea and always in distress.

The certificated operator is in charge of the set; crew use it under supervision, and anyone may call in distress. Coast stations announce weather on 16 and read it on a working channel. The handheld, for dinghy and liferaft, needs its charger.

**DSC** needs the boat's MMSI programmed and the cover on the red button. When an alert comes in, listen on 16 and note the position: the coast station answers; you call only if nobody does and you can help.

sections.title: Which switches go on, and when

blocks.p: With the engine driving you are a power-driven vessel, sails up or not. Under sail alone show the tricolour or the deck-level lights, never both. At anchor show the all-round white only: sidelights mean under way. Deck light off: it blinds the helm. A vessel of 12 m or more carries a whistle: the electric horn, with the aerosol can as the spare. Test both.
